Hawaiian dascyllus, Dascyllus albisella, is a common damselfish inhabiting coral reefs throughout the Hawaiian archipelago. Newly hatched prolarvae emerge from demersal eggs after a brief incubation period; at a stable temperature of 20.3 °C [T = 20.3 °C], eclosion occurs approximately 8 days [ab = approximately 8 days] following fertilisation. The yolk-sac larva at this stage measures just over half a millimeter in length and possesses a wet weight at birth of 0.000091 grams [Wwb = 0.000091 grams], a mass derived from eggs that are approximately 0.7 millimeters in length and 0.5 millimeters in width. These tiny, endotrophic larvae rely entirely on their yolk reserves during the first few days post-hatching before the mouth opens and the exotrophic transition begins. The timing of hatching is tightly linked to thermal conditions, and the values reported here were all recorded under controlled laboratory conditions at the specified temperature.

As juveniles progress through the post-settlement phase and approach sexual maturation, several key morphological benchmarks become apparent. The standard length at which puberty is initiated has been determined to be 6 centimeters [Lp = 6 centimeters], a size typically reached during the first year of benthic life. Corresponding to this length, the wet weight at puberty is approximately 4.4 grams [Wwp = approximately 4.4 grams], reflecting the substantial somatic growth that occurs as the juvenile transitions from a planktonic to a reef-associated existence. This weight, while modest, represents a considerable increase from the neonatal mass and underscores the rapid early growth phase characteristic of this species. Reaching these developmental milestones is prerequisite for the activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal (HPG) axis and the onset of vitellogenesis in females and spermatogenesis in males.

Sexually mature adults of Hawaiian dascyllus continue to grow, albeit at a decelerated rate, until they approach their ultimate size. The maximum or ultimate standard length recorded for this species is 13 centimeters [Li = 13 centimeters], a value that represents the asymptotic length attained well after the initiation of reproductive activity. At this terminal size, the corresponding ultimate wet weight of a fully grown adult is 43.6 grams [Wwi = 43.6 grams], a body mass that places it among the larger members of its genus in the region. This asymptotic mass is achieved only after several years of growth and is consistent with the allometric relationship derived from length-weight regressions for this species. The attainment of this maximum size signals a shift in energy investment away from somatic growth and toward the maintenance of reproductive output over the remainder of the adult lifespan.

Reproductive effort in Dascyllus albisella is considerable, with females capable of producing multiple clutches over an extended spawning season. At the same stable temperature of 20.3 °C [T = 20.3 °C] used for the incubation studies, the maximum reproductive output has been quantified. Females produce an average clutch size of approximately 145 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 145 eggs per spawning event], and they can spawn on a near-daily basis, with a frequency of roughly one spawning event per day [F_R_i = roughly one spawning event per day] during peak reproductive periods. This combination of moderate clutch size and very high spawning frequency results in a substantial lifetime fecundity, although the exact number of eggs produced annually is subject to variation based on female body condition and food availability. Such a reproductive strategy is typical of many small, iteroparous reef fishes that face high juvenile mortality.

The complete life cycle of the Hawaiian dascyllus unfolds over a considerable period, with the maximum recorded lifespan documented under controlled thermal conditions. At the species-typical temperature of 20.3 °C [T = 20.3 °C], the oldest individuals have been observed to survive for 5110 days [am = 5110 days], which is equivalent to approximately 14 years. This relatively extended longevity, unusual for a fish of this modest body size, is likely linked to the stable, predator-rich environment of Hawaiian coral reefs and a life-history strategy that emphasizes repeated reproductive events over many years. The oldest fish typically exhibit signs of reproductive senescence in their final years, with a gradual decline in clutch size and spawning frequency before eventual natural mortality. This lifespan, coupled with the species’ high fecundity and rapid early growth, allows Dascyllus albisella to maintain stable populations across its restricted geographic range.
